html:
A fortified old town on a headland at Galle, on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka. The Portuguese built the first fort in 1588; the Dutch took it in 1640 and from 1663 built most of the stone walls that stand today.

Galle was a natural harbour on the sea routes from Arabia and India to Southeast Asia. Under the Dutch East India Company it was the chief port of Dutch Ceylon, shipping cinnamon and other goods (see Dutch Ceylon and cinnamon). The Dutch built bastions, a grid of streets, churches, warehouses and a clever sewer that the tide flushed out.

The British took it in 1796 and later moved the main port to Colombo. Galle kept its old shape: a living town of houses, shops and mosques inside the ramparts. When the 2004 tsunami devastated the city around it, the old walls largely protected the town within. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1988, one of the best kept European forts in Asia.
sum: A fortified old town on a headland at Galle, on the southwest coast of Sri Lanka. The Portuguese built the first fort in 1588; the Dutch took it in 1640 and from 1663 built most of the stone walls that stand today.
